info.bio: The Sister Of Mercy es una de las bandas más reconocidas y que destaca muy por encima de la segunda oleada de rock gótico. El grupo  tomó el nombre de una canción del cantautor Leonard Cohen; se formaron en Leeds, Inglaterra, en 1980 de la mano de Andrew Eldritch (voz, nacido como Andrew Taylor) y Gary Marx (guitarra, nacido como Mark Pairman) con la ayuda de una caja de ritmos, la mítica Doktor Avalanche. Originalmente se usó una DR-55, después

scenes.name: Gótico
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Término que Hannett aplicó a Joy Division y luego insulto para los epígonos, hasta que en 1982 los fans lo adoptan como estandarte frente a la excesiva luminosidad del new pop: glamour sepulcral, retorno de lo reprimido, emociones atemporales. Bauhaus («Bela Lugosi's Dead», 1979, el comienzo propiamente dicho; Peter Murphy, sex symbol heredero de Adam Ant y Bowie), The Birthday Party (el gótico americano de Nick Cave: «Release the Bats», Junkyard), Killing Joke («música de tensión», del funk de PiL a Black Sabbath, con un aura inquietante), The Cure (gótico light: Seventeen Seconds, Faith, Pornography). El club The Batcave (1982), el «positive punk», Southern Death Cult, Theatre of Hate, The Sisters of Mercy («¡Nosotros sí somos una banda de rock!»), el death rock de Los Ángeles y Kukl con Björk. Su deriva: coqueteos totalitarios y la conversión en versión postpunk del heavy metal (The Cult).

scenes.name: Dark punk y rock gótico
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El punk británico estuvo flanqueado desde el principio por un movimiento «gótico» que canalizaba su violencia hacia atmósferas de terror y rituales esotéricos: Stranglers, Siouxsie, X-Ray Spex. Lo más interesante evita el tono de película de terror: The Cure introducen la angustia existencial de Camus y Sartre (Pornography, Disintegration); Joy Division mezclan Doors, Kraftwerk y Black Sabbath y su final anuncia el synth-pop; Bauhaus, Killing Joke, Psychedelic Furs, los irlandeses Virgin Prunes y la cima del género, Public Image Ltd de Johnny Lydon, que convierte el punk en música de cámara con dub y ecos étnicos (Second Edition, Flowers Of Romance). Después, el gótico bailable de Sisters Of Mercy, Alien Sex Fiend, Cult, Mission e In The Nursery.

podcast.body: The Sisters of Mercy are among the artists who have covered The Stooges' song "1969." "Tracks on this album have been covered by the Sex Pistols, Joey Ramone, Sonic Youth, the Sisters of Mercy, Joan Jett, Red Cross, and the Black Keys."

srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Formation in Leeds (1980)
podcast.body: Formed in Leeds in 1980 during the earliest days of goth, The Sisters of Mercy became one of the most important bands in the genre, known for their unique blend of doom and gloom with a rock sensibility. "They were formed in Leeds in 1980 during the earliest days of Goth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Roots of Modern Gothic Music (1987)
podcast.body: The Sisters of Mercy, specifically with a song from 1987, are used to illustrate the historical lineage of modern gothic music. The roots of this compositional style are traced back over 800 years to Hildegard von Bingen's sacred monophony, composed around 1156, and its suitability for performance in massive stone cathedrals. "Yes, that's the systems of mercy from 1987, but the roots of that kind of composition go back to 1156."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Dr. Abelash" Drum Machine
podcast.body: The Sisters of Mercy toured with a drum machine they humorously nicknamed "Dr. Abelash." The name was given because the machine frequently crashed during performances, highlighting the early unreliability of such technology. "The sisters of Mercy toured with a box they called Dr. Abelash because it kept crashing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Andrew Eldritch's Vocal Style
podcast.body: Frontman Andrew Eldritch was known for his deep, baritone voice, described as a "voice of doom," which became a signature element of the band's sound. "Out front was Andrew Eldridge, with his deep, baritone voice of doom."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Jim Steinman
podcast.body: In the late 1980s, the band collaborated with songwriter Jim Steinman, known for his work with Meat Loaf and Bonnie Tyler, to infuse their doom and gloom with an interesting rock dynamic. "That was most evident in the late 1980s when they teamed up with songwriter Jim Steinman, the guy behind Meatloaf's Battle of Hell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Declared Influence
podcast.body: Sisters of Mercy is among a partial list of artists and bands who have publicly stated that they have been influenced by Joy Division in some way. "You too, arcade fire, smashing pumpkins, nine inch nails, to pesh mode, sisters of mercy, ministry, chain addiction, the smiths, Bjork, Jesus and Marychain, Moby, primal scream, the Charlotains, Interpol, editors, white lies, Frans Ferdinand. I could go on, but I think you get the point."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Dr. Avalanche's Unique Name
podcast.body: Their drum machine, Dr. Avalanche, earned its name because it frequently crashed. There have been multiple "Dr. Avalanches" over time, including various Roland models and a custom MacBook. "Somewhere at the back was drummer Dr. Avalanche. He drum machine the gutt its name because it kept, well, crashing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Covers
podcast.body: In their early days, The Sisters of Mercy were known for covering songs by artists such as The Stooges, Bob Dylan, "not chocolate if I'm a band," The Velvet Underground, and a "killer version of Louis Louis." "But in the early days, the Sisters were known for their covers, stooges, bob Dylan, not chocolate if I'm a band, velvet underground, and a killer version of Louis Louis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major 90s Goth Band
podcast.body: Sisters of Mercy were identified as one of the major Goth bands of the 1990s, a genre that often incorporated elements of the occult and the bizarre, extending its culture to clubs and magazines beyond just the music. "The major goth bands of the 90s were Bauhaus and Suzy and the Banshee's, Sisters of Mercy, and if we go back to the very beginning we'll find that Joy Division was a major influence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Many Ex-Members
podcast.body: The band is notable for having had nearly 20 ex-members, in addition to a succession of drum machines (Dr. Avalanche models), indicating a frequent turnover in its lineup. "Those are really the only members you need to know because there were close to 20 X members of the Sisters of Mercy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Name Origin and Leonard Cohen Influence
podcast.body: The band took its name from Leonard Cohen's song "Sisters of Mercy." Cohen's dark material also found favor with some goths, linking his work to the band's aesthetic. "And then there's his song Sisters of Mercy, from which the band took their name."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Second Generation Goth Influence
podcast.body: The band was instrumental in carrying Goth music beyond its UK birthplace by the mid-1980s, alongside Siouxsie and the Banshees and The Cure. "It was carried on the wings of music, sisters of mercy, suzzy in the banshees and the cure."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

concerts.title: Co-headlining Tour with Public Enemy
concerts.body: The Sisters of Mercy, described as "one of the greatest Goth bands of all time," agreed to a co-headlining tour with Public Enemy, a move that contributed to the spread of hip-hop and rap. "Even the Sisters of Mercy, one of the greatest Goth bands of all time, contributed to this spread of hip-hop and rap by agreeing to a co-headlining tour with public enemy."

xref.body: Along with The Cure, The Sisters of Mercy, Siouxsie and the Banshees, and Joy Division, Bauhaus records were a significant part of "second generation Goth" in the latter half of the 1980s. "Along with the cure and the sister of mercy, choosing the banshees and some immortal Bauhaus and joy division records, there were a series of other bands that, well not exactly big in the mainstream, were huge parts of the cult of the Goth."
